note: Screening quick-reference for serious spinal pathology. Summarised from named frameworks and studies; check the source before relying on any single item. Not a substitute for clinical judgement or local referral pathways.
principles: Few red flags are informative on their own. Interpret them in combination, within a full history and examination, and against the person's profile (age, sex, history).

Set an index of suspicion from low to high, then choose an action: no concerning features → trial of therapy; few → therapy with watchful waiting and close monitoring; some → don't start therapy, investigate further or refer urgently; high → don't start therapy, refer as an emergency.
Safety-net whenever serious pathology is possible but not confirmed: what to watch for, what to do, and how quickly.
Explain why you're asking screening questions, and follow local emergency and urgent referral pathways.

conditions.name: Cauda equina syndrome
risk_factors: Large central disc herniation, commonly L4–5 or L5–S1
Age under 50
Obesity
Lumbar spinal stenosis
Any previous lumbar spinal surgery
symptoms: Unilateral or bilateral radicular pain
Progression from unilateral to bilateral, or alternating, leg pain
Saddle sensory disturbance
Bladder or bowel disturbance, urinary retention or incontinence
Sexual dysfunction
signs: Saddle sensory deficit to light touch and pinprick
Reduced anal tone (assessed in secondary care)
conditions.action: Suspected CES: emergency MRI and surgical opinion. If CES isn't present but could develop, safety-net clearly (what symptoms mean go to ED now).

conditions.name: Spinal fracture
risk_factors: Osteoporosis, or a family history of it
Previous osteoporotic or spinal fracture
Corticosteroid use
Previous cancer (breast, prostate, lung, kidney, thyroid)
Significant trauma or fall from height
Female sex, especially early menopause or late menarche; older age; falls history
Heavy alcohol use, smoking, vitamin D deficiency, rheumatoid arthritis
symptoms: Sudden-onset thoracolumbar pain after low-impact trauma
Severe or unfamiliar pain
Neurological symptoms (bilateral, gait, bladder or bowel changes)
conditions.action: Don't act on a single red flag. Low risk: treat and monitor. High-risk older person with progressive pain: urgent X-ray. Multiple concerning features or suspected malignancy: urgent whole-spine MRI.

conditions.name: Spinal malignancy / metastatic spinal cord compression
risk_factors: Past history of cancer, especially breast, prostate, lung, kidney or thyroid (higher with advanced stage, large tumours, lymph node involvement)
About a quarter of people with MSCC have no known primary cancer
Older age
symptoms: Severe, progressive or constant pain
Band-like pain
Pain worse lying flat; night pain not eased by changing position
Systemic symptoms suggesting hypercalcaemia
Unexplained weight loss (more than 5% in 6 months)
Neurological symptoms
signs: Altered sensation from the trunk down
Spinal tenderness (its absence does not rule out metastasis)
conditions.action: Concerning features: urgent whole-spine MRI. Suspected MSCC: emergency MRI. Blood tests can't reliably rule malignancy in or out. Safety-net.

conditions.name: Spinal infection
risk_factors: Intravenous drug use
Recent spinal procedure (post-procedural discitis is up to 30% of cases)
Older age
HIV/AIDS or tuberculosis
Infection with Staphylococcus aureus or Brucella
conditions.action: Rare and often missed; discitis most often affects the lumbar spine. The symptom, sign and action tables for infection weren't checked for this card. Read Tables 18–21 of the framework before relying on it.

conditions.name: Cervical arterial dysfunction (vertebrobasilar or internal carotid)
risk_factors: Recent trauma (including mild to moderate, and recent manual therapy)
Vascular anomaly, family history of stroke
Smoking, hypertension, high cholesterol
Migraine, recent infection, oral contraceptive use
Absence of risk factors does NOT rule it out: spontaneous dissection happens
symptoms: Acute neck pain or headache that is unusual for this person
Visual disturbance; paraesthesia of the face or limbs; dizziness
Vertebrobasilar: unsteadiness or ataxia, dysarthria or dysphasia, dysphagia, nausea or vomiting, limb weakness, facial palsy, drowsiness or confusion
Internal carotid: ptosis (often ipsilateral), facial palsy, upper or lower limb weakness, dysphasia
signs: Upper motor neuron signs; cranial nerve dysfunction
Unusually high blood pressure, interpreted with other findings
Carotid pulse asymmetry, pulsatile mass or bruit (a normal exam doesn't exclude dissection)
conditions.action: Suspicion supported by history and exam: refer for immediate medical investigation and don't treat with manual therapy. Provocative positional (VBI) testing is no longer recommended. Also consider giant cell arteritis, thunderclap headache (RCVS, subarachnoid haemorrhage) and upper cervical instability.

conditions.name: Cervical myelopathy
risk_factors: Age over 45
symptoms: Gait change: wide-based, ataxic or spastic gait
signs: Cluster of 5: gait deviation, positive Hoffmann's, inverted supinator sign, positive Babinski, age over 45
1 of 5 positive helps rule out (LR− about 0.18); 3 of 5 positive strongly rules in (LR+ about 31)
conditions.action: A positive cluster warrants medical referral and imaging. The cluster numbers here come from a secondary summary and weren't checked against the original paper; confirm before quoting.

conditions.name: Neck trauma: does it need imaging? (Canadian C-spine rule)
risk_factors: High risk (image): age 65 or over, dangerous mechanism, or paraesthesias in the limbs
symptoms: Low risk (allows range-of-motion assessment): simple rear-end MVC, sitting position in ED, ambulatory at any time since injury, delayed onset of neck pain, or no midline C-spine tenderness
signs: If low risk is present: can they actively rotate 45° left and right? If yes, no imaging needed; if no, image
conditions.action: For alert (GCS 15), stable adults after blunt trauma. In the derivation cohort of 8,924 adults it was 100% sensitive for clinically important C-spine injury (specificity 42.5%).
